overview.headline: Plutonium origins, radiation, isotopes, decay and reactor uses

keyPoints.point: Plutonium forms inside a reactor after uranium atoms absorb neutrons during operation
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium is created in a reactor when uranium atoms absorb neutrons.

keyPoints.point: Plutonium emits alpha particles as radiation that is easily stopped over a short range
keyPoints.quote: Plutonium predominantly emits alpha particles – a type of radiation that is easily stopped and has a short range.

keyPoints.point: Isotopes have distinct half-life values measured in years with shorter half-life material decaying quickly
keyPoints.quote: Pu-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years and Pu-241’s half-life is 14.4 years.

keyPoints.point: Reprocessing uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium for mixed oxide fuel production
keyPoints.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.

keyTerms.gloss: radioactive metallic element that is nearly all man-made
type of radiation that is easily stopped and has short range
keyTerms.quote: Plutonium predominantly emits alpha particles – a type of radiation that is easily stopped and has a short range.

keyTerms.gloss: common forms of plutonium listed by mass number
keyTerms.quote: There are five “common” isotopes of plutonium, Pu-238, Pu-239, Pu-240, Pu-241, and Pu-242.

keyTerms.gloss: time it takes to lose half of its radioactivity through decay
keyTerms.quote: The different isotopes have different “half-lives” – the time it takes to lose half of its radioactivity.

keyTerms.gloss: process that uses chemicals to separate plutonium from spent fuel
keyTerms.quote: This process, known as reprocessing, uses chemicals to separate plutonium from uranium and other fission products.
